lead: On the eve of Denha the readings are sober. The letter to Titus insists that those who believe must devote themselves to good works, and warns against quarrels. In the Gospel, Jesus replies to a curious question about numbers by telling the questioner to strive for the narrow door. Before the feast of Baptism, both readings ask how seriously we take the life we entered through that door.

set: Titus is presented as Paul’s co-worker, left on Crete to organise the churches (1:5). This is one of the Pastoral Letters, which the Church receives among Paul’s letters; many scholars think that they come from a disciple writing in his name, while others defend Paul’s own authorship. V. 8 comes straight after one of the letter’s great statements about the grace of Baptism (3:4–7).
str: v. 8: the saying is sure; believers must do good works.
v. 9: stay away from useless disputes.
vv. 10–11: how to deal with one who divides the community.
kw: A formula found only in the Pastoral Letters (for example 1 Timothy 1:15), pointing to a teaching held firmly by the Church.
Literally “beautiful” or “excellent” works. Salvation is not by works (3:5), yet the saved are to devote themselves to them. Grace bears fruit.
The word that later gave us “heretic”. Here it has its earlier sense: a person who makes factions. The later technical meaning should not be read back into it.
vv: I desire that you insist on these things, so that those who have come to believe in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works
The word for “devote” suggests taking the lead in something. Good works are not a side matter.
But avoid stupid controversies, genealogies, dissensions, and quarrels about the law, for they are unprofitable and worthless.
We do not know exactly what these disputes on Crete were. The test Titus is given is a practical one: does this argument build anyone up?
ch: The Catechism recalls that “faith apart from works is dead” (CCC 1815). It defines heresy as the obstinate denial of a truth of faith after Baptism (CCC 2089), and it says that those born today into communities separated from the Catholic Church cannot be charged with the sin of separation; the Church accepts them with respect and affection as brothers and sisters (CCC 818). The letter’s severity is about protecting the community’s unity, not about hating a person.

r.h: Strive to enter through the narrow door
set: Jesus is making his way to Jerusalem (13:22). Someone asks him about numbers. Jesus does not give a figure; he turns a question about others into a warning for the questioner. Matthew has a similar saying about the narrow gate (Matthew 7:13–14) and the people from east and west (8:11–12); Luke puts them together here as a picture of a house whose owner shuts the door.
str: v. 23: “will only a few be saved?”
vv. 25–27: the shut door: “We ate and drank with you”; “I do not know where you come from”.
vv. 28–29: those shut out and the banquet with people from everywhere.
v. 30: the last and the first.
kw: From agōn, the contest or struggle of an athlete. The verb is in the present tense: keep striving. The word points to effort, not to anxiety.
A door one must enter deliberately, not a wide road one drifts along. In John, Jesus calls himself the gate, the same Greek word thyra (John 10:9).
vv: Strive to enter through the narrow door; for many, I tell you, will try to enter and will not be able.
The failure lies in coming too late or wanting to come without change.
We ate and drank with you, and you taught in our streets.
Being near Jesus is not the same as following him. This warning reaches every believer, and it reaches us who eat at his table in the Holy Qurbana.
Then people will come from east and west, from north and south, and will eat in the kingdom of God.

Isaiah promised such a feast for all peoples (Isaiah 25:6). Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and the prophets are already at the table (13:28). The warning is not about any one nation; it is for all who assume that their place is safe.
ch: The Catechism quotes the saying about the narrow gate as a call to take responsibility for our eternal destiny (CCC 1036). It also says that the Church prays that no one should be lost (CCC 1058), and it teaches that those who through no fault of their own do not know the Gospel, yet seek God sincerely, can attain salvation (CCC 847; Lumen Gentium 16). Everyone is called to enter the Kingdom (CCC 543). So the Church holds both things: God’s wide mercy and each person’s real responsibility.

qa: Does this Gospel say that only a few will be saved?

Jesus refuses to give a number. What he does say is that entering takes effort, that it cannot be assumed, and that people will come from all directions. The Church does not say how many are saved, and she prays for all (CCC 1058).
rite: The eve of Denha had its own custom among Kerala’s Christians: rakkuli, the bath at night in river or pond, recalling the Jordan. Whether or not a family keeps this today, the eve is a good time to remember one’s own Baptism, the door through which each of us has already been brought.
study: Am I more interested in how others will fare with God than in my own response to him?
“We ate and drank with you”. How can I keep my reception of the Holy Qurbana from becoming a mere habit?
